readerTitle: Is cost plus 30% a good price?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 빵집, 소프트웨어 구독 서비스) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 원가는 가격을 정하는 답이 아니라 바닥을 확인하는 도구다. 단위 원가 자체가 판매량 예측에 기대고 있기 때문이다.
misconception: 원가에 일정 마진을 붙이면 손해 볼 일이 없는 안전한 가격이 된다.

sources.text: 관리회계의 표준 개념 (원가가산 가격결정, 고정비 배분, 수요 감소 악순환)

factChecks.note: 'death spiral'(수요 감소 악순환)은 관리회계 교재에서 쓰이는 일반 용어입니다. 원가가산 계약이 판매자의 비용 절감 동기를 약하게 만든다는 점은 건설·공공 조달 분야에서 널리 지적되는 일반론으로만 서술했습니다. 특정 사례나 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Is cost plus 30% a good price?
body: A baker works out that each sourdough loaf costs $3.50 to make. She adds 30% and prices it at $4.55.
It feels safe. Every loaf covers its cost, plus a bit. But that $3.50 is built on a guess, and the guess can turn the formula against her.

image.label: A sourdough loaf with a price tag reading cost plus 30%
image.brief: 따뜻한 톤의 동네 빵집 카운터. 사워도우 빵 한 덩이에 "$3.50 + 30% = $4.55"라고 적힌 손글씨 가격표. 가격표 뒤에 작은 물음표 그림자. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Sales came in lower than planned.
body: Ingredients cost $1.50 a loaf. Rent share, oven and baker time cost $3,000 a month. She planned on 1,500 loaves, so each loaf "cost" $3.50 and sold for $4.55.
She sold only 1,000. Re-running her formula, each loaf now "costs" $4.50, so cost plus 30% says $5.85. What should she do?

options.text: Follow the formula and raise the price to $5.85
options.feedback: It might hold if customers barely notice. But she's raising the price because fewer people bought, and if sales drop again, the formula will ask her to raise it again.

options.text: Keep $4.55 and find out why sales are low and what customers would pay
options.feedback: At 1,000 loaves she still clears about $50, so there's time to learn. The cost tells her the floor; customers tell her the price.

options.text: Cut to $3.99 to win more customers
options.feedback: More volume does lower the cost per loaf. But each loaf now leaves $2.49, so she needs about 1,205 loaves a month just to cover the $3,000.

cards.title: Same loaf, two different "costs".
body: Nothing changed in the kitchen. Only the sales guess changed. Fewer sales made each loaf look more expensive, so the formula pushed the price **up** just when demand was weak.

cards.title: Cost-plus pricing
body: **Cost-plus pricing** means working out what one unit costs you, then adding a fixed markup. Cost $3.50, markup 30%, price $4.55.
It's popular for good reasons. It's quick, easy to explain, and easy to defend to a customer. Caterers, contractors, print shops and manufacturers use it every day.
Its promise is that every sale covers its cost. That promise only holds if the sales you planned actually show up.

image.label: Cost block stacked with a markup block to form the price
image.brief: 블록 쌓기 인포그래픽. 아래 큰 블록 "Cost per unit", 위에 작은 블록 "Markup 30%", 합쳐서 "Price". 아래 블록 안에 "depends on how many you sell"이라는 작은 주석과 점선.

cards.title: The hidden circle.
body: Cost per unit depends on how many you sell. How many you sell depends on price. So cost-plus quietly assumes the answer it's trying to find.
When sales fall, fixed costs spread over fewer units, the "cost" rises, and the price rises with it. That can cut sales again. Accountants call this the **death spiral**.
The formula also never looks at the customer. A loaf people would happily buy at $6 gets priced at $4.55. One they'd only buy at $4 gets priced higher and sits on the shelf.

image.label: A loop: fewer sales, higher unit cost, higher price, fewer sales
image.brief: 원형 화살표 다이어그램 4단계: "Fewer sales" → "Higher cost per unit" → "Higher price" → "Fewer sales". 화살표가 아래로 소용돌이치듯 점점 작아지는 느낌. 차분한 색, 과장된 경고 표시 없음.

cards.title: Where cost-plus earns its place.
body: Cost-plus works best when costs are hard to predict and the buyer accepts that. A custom renovation or a one-off catering job is often priced as cost plus a fee, because nobody knows the full cost upfront.
It also works as a **floor check**. Before you set any price, cost tells you the lowest number that keeps the business alive at a realistic volume.
Where it struggles: products with high fixed costs, uncertain volume, or customers who value them far above or below your cost.

cards.title: The markup can reward the wrong thing.
body: When a contract pays cost plus a percentage, the seller earns more by spending more. There's little reason to find a cheaper supplier or a faster method. Buyers often push for a fixed fee or a cap for this reason.
And the markup itself is usually a habit, not a decision. 30% isn't right because it's round. It's right only if customers will pay it and your volume covers your fixed costs.

cards.title: Now it's a software subscription.
body: Your team costs $40,000 a month. Hosting and support cost about $4 per customer. You expect 2,000 customers, so each one "costs" $24. Cost plus 30% gives $31.20 a month.
How should you use that number?

options.text: Charge $31.20. It covers every cost with a margin
options.feedback: It works if users arrive. You break even at about 1,471 customers, so the price rests on a sign-up forecast you haven't tested.

options.text: Charge $5.20, since one more customer only costs $4
options.feedback: Each sale covers its own cost, but you'd need about 33,000 customers just to pay the team. A floor for one sale isn't a price for a business.

options.text: Treat $24 as a viability check, set the price from what customers get, then check the volume needed
options.feedback: You keep cost in its useful role: a test of whether the business can work. The price itself comes from customers, not from your spreadsheet.

cards.title: Cost tells you the floor, not the price.
body: Cost-plus is simple and defensible, but its "cost" depends on a sales guess, and it never asks what customers will pay.
**Try it today:** pick one product. Work out its cost per unit at your expected volume, then at 30% lower volume. If the price swings a lot, your price is resting on a guess.
